# 2020 Jonesboro tornado
The 2020 Jonesboro tornado was a destructive EF3 tornado that struck the city of Jonesboro, Arkansas on March 28, 2020. The tornado touched down in the southeastern part of Jonesboro around 5:00 p.m. local time and carved a path roughly 12.5 miles (20 km) long across the city. It caused widespread damage to homes, businesses, and infrastructure, injuring 22 people but causing no fatalities. Major landmarks damaged included The Mall at Turtle Creek – the city’s primary shopping mall – and the Jonesboro Municipal Airport. Officials noted that the low casualty count was aided by timely warnings and the fact that many normally busy facilities were closed or sparsely occupied due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
## Meteorological background
On March 28, 2020, a significant severe weather outbreak was underway across parts of the Midwest and South. The Storm Prediction Center had forecast a risk of tornadoes that day, and several twisters were reported in Arkansas, Illinois, and Iowa. In Arkansas, a supercell thunderstorm developed during the afternoon and first produced a weaker tornado (rated EF1) in Jackson County, southeast of Jonesboro. This same storm intensified as it moved northeast toward Craighead County. The National Weather Service office in Memphis issued a tornado warning for the Jonesboro area by 4:47 p.m., and within minutes the storm generated a tornado on the south side of the city near Interstate 555.
As the tornado entered Jonesboro shortly before 5 p.m., it rapidly strengthened. Doppler radar indicated a strong velocity couplet as the storm approached the city, and observers captured video of a large funnel cloud moving through town. The tornado tracked roughly north-northeast through southern and eastern sections of Jonesboro, remaining on the ground for an estimated 15 to 20 minutes. The National Weather Service rated the tornado EF3, with peak winds around 140 mph (225 km/h). The damage swath reached up to about 500–600 meters in width at its peak intensity. This was the strongest tornado to affect Arkansas since the April 27, 2014 outbreak, which included an EF4 tornado in Vilonia.
## Impact and damage
The tornado caused severe and widespread damage across Jonesboro. It initially struck a commercial area on the city’s south side, heavily damaging The Mall at Turtle Creek. The nearly empty mall – normally busy on a Saturday – suffered major structural damage, with numerous stores destroyed or left in ruins. The twister then crossed residential neighborhoods and an industrial corridor as it moved toward the northeast. Dozens of houses were flattened or lost their roofs and exterior walls, and vehicles were tossed into piles of debris. At the Jonesboro Municipal Airport, the tornado reached its maximum intensity (EF3) – hangars were obliterated, several small airplanes were mangled, and an anemometer recorded a wind gust of 74 mph before failing. Just north of the airport, railcars were pushed off the tracks as a freight train was derailed by the winds. In total, approximately 300 buildings in Jonesboro were damaged or destroyed by the tornado. Power lines and trees were downed across the city, causing widespread outages and blocking roads with debris.
Despite the extensive destruction, no one was killed in the Jonesboro tornado. About 22 people were reported injured, and most of those injuries were minor. Only two people required hospitalization, and both sustained non-life-threatening injuries. The lack of fatalities was considered remarkably fortunate, given that the tornado struck a densely populated area on a weekend afternoon. City officials attributed the low number of casualties in part to the COVID-19 pandemic timing: many businesses had closed early or were entirely shut down, resulting in far fewer people at places like the mall when the storm hit. Jonesboro’s mayor Harold Perrin noted that under normal circumstances “a lot more people” would have been in the tornado’s path at the mall and elsewhere, potentially leading to a much worse outcome. The local E-911 director described the situation as a “blessing in disguise” in terms of preventing injuries. Advanced warning also played a role – the National Weather Service warning issued about 10 minutes before touchdown gave many residents time to seek shelter after hearing sirens and alerts.
## Aftermath and response
In the immediate aftermath of the tornado, authorities in Jonesboro implemented emergency measures to assist victims and keep residents safe. A citywide curfew was enacted on the evening of March 28 to keep people off the streets and allow first responders to conduct search and rescue operations. Emergency crews and volunteers fanned out to the hardest-hit areas to check for anyone trapped in damaged buildings. Fortunately, no fatalities or life-threatening injuries meant the response focused on securing hazards and providing shelter. The Jonesboro police and local relief organizations opened four emergency shelters to accommodate those displaced by the tornado. The Arkansas Army National Guard delivered cots and supplies to support these shelters overnight. Residents were urged to continue observing pandemic-related social distancing even as they sought shelter and assistance, complicating the usual relief efforts.
On March 29, Arkansas Governor Asa Hutchinson declared a state disaster for the Jonesboro area, mobilizing state resources for recovery and formally requesting federal assistance. In a statement, the governor remarked that he had not seen such tornado devastation in the state during his tenure, comparing it to prior major disasters. Since the tornado struck amid the COVID-19 crisis, state officials noted that businesses destroyed by the storm would be eligible for federal disaster loans already in place for the pandemic. Damage assessments in the days following the event indicated that the tornado had inflicted massive property losses. Early surveys by the Red Cross found dozens of homes completely demolished (55 destroyed in just the initial 35% of the damage assessment). Overall, local officials estimated “several hundred million dollars” in total damage costs to the Jonesboro area. Governor Hutchinson stated that the damage likely met the threshold for a federal disaster declaration, and federal aid was later approved to support rebuilding efforts.
Reconstruction in Jonesboro proceeded in the months and years after the tornado, though full recovery took time. Many damaged homes and businesses were rebuilt or repaired, but some facilities never returned. In particular, The Mall at Turtle Creek, which had been a centerpiece of the city’s retail community, was permanently closed as a result of the tornado’s destruction. Several of the mall’s retailers later relocated to other shopping centers or rebuilt at new locations in the city, but the mall structure itself was not restored. By the one-year anniversary of the disaster, most of the debris had been cleared and many affected neighborhoods were on the mend, even as the community coped with the dual challenges of tornado recovery and the ongoing pandemic. City leaders praised the efficient warning systems and community response that helped prevent loss of life, and Jonesboro’s experience in 2020 has since been cited as a case study in effective emergency preparedness during compounding disasters.

A screen grab from a social media video shows a tornado tearing through Jonesboro, Ark., on Saturday.

A tornado tore through nearly 20 miles of the city of Jonesboro, Ark., on Saturday evening, severely damaging multiple properties and injuring at least 22 people, according to local news reports.

Videos and photos posted to social media show [extensive damage](https://twitter.com/_JurneeTaylor/status/1244030178751373314?s=20) to large swaths of the city, including to a [municipal airport](https://twitter.com/D1Jonesboro/status/1244068741408792581?s=20) and a local shopping mall. But despite the strength of the tornado, there have been no reports of fatalities and city officials attribute that, and the relatively low number of injuries, in part to the social distancing guidelines and business closures caused by the coronavirus pandemic.

"Had we not had that here now, I would say you would have had a lot more people in that mall and we would have had a much worse situation than we have now," Jonesboro Mayor Harold Perrin told [local television station KAIT 8](https://www.kait8.com/2020/03/28/tornado-warnings-issued-throughout-region-craighead-poinsett-counties-pm/).

Another local official, Jonesboro E-911 Director Jeff Presley [reportedly said](https://apnews.com/673fcfce288fb32f197c48963ce5d620) the circumstances were a "blessing in disguise."

Though Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson has [urged Arkansas residents to stay home](https://twitter.com/AsaHutchinson/status/1243541141074690061?s=20) whenever possible to prevent the spread of the coronavirus, he [has not ordered](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2020/us/coronavirus-stay-at-home-order.html) the state's non-essential businesses to close or ordered residents to stay at home, an action which [has been taken](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2020/us/coronavirus-stay-at-home-order.html) in at least 26 states. Perrin, who ordered a 7 p.m. curfew after the tornado, said that people in his city have been taking the pandemic seriously. Jonesboro, located about 130 miles northeast of Little Rock, is home to more than 75,000 people.

Jonesboro Police Chief Rick Elliott echoed Perrin's sentiments that actions taken to curb the pandemic may have helped the city avoid a larger injury count, but he also urged residents to continue social distancing despite the crisis, specifically saying not to leave their homes in the aftermath of the tornado to survey the damage it wrought.

"Stay in shelter, which you should be doing anyway, and be thankful that it wasn't worse than what we're looking at," Elliott told KAIT 8. The police department also [opened four shelters](https://www.facebook.com/pg/TheJonesboroPD/posts/?ref=page_internal) throughout the city to house people affected.

Several other tornadoes [were reported Saturday](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/exper/reports/?&all&date=20200328) in other parts of Arkansas, as well as Iowa and Illinois, according to the National Weather Service. Earlier that day, the Weather Service had warned of [severe weather in the Midwest](https://www.washingtonpost.com/weather/2020/03/28/severe-thunderstorms-tornadoes-midwest/) and down the Mississippi Valley.

Though the pandemic closures may have kept people safe by keeping them away from the commercial center where the Jonesboro tornado hit, staying at home may not always be the safest place during a tornado if a home's structure isn't sturdy. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [recommends moving to a basement](https://www.cdc.gov/nceh/features/tornadosafety/index.html) or inside room without windows, and to seek shelter in a nearby building if you live in a mobile home.

31.title: Picking Up the Pieces—Carefully—after an EF3 Tornado in Arkansas
31.description: Coronavirus-related closures may have saved lives in Jonesboro, but they are also complicating recovery efforts.
31.content:
_**Above:**_ _This photo from the Mall at Turtle Creek in Jonesboro, Arkansas, from Sunday, March 29, 2020, shows severe damage inflicted by a tornado late Saturday, March 28. (_[_Jonesboro Police Department_](https://www.facebook.com/TheJonesboroPD/photos/pcb.534831167425802/534827574092828/?type=3&theater)_via Facebook)_

The first U.S. weather disaster of the coronavirus-shutdown era hit the northeast Arkansas city of Jonesboro on Saturday afternoon. A tornado rated as EF3 by the National Weather Service office in Memphis tore across southern and eastern Jonesboro around 5 pm CDT. Top winds were estimated at 140 mph along a 12.6-mile path.

The Jonesboro tornado emerged from an intense, fast-moving supercell that had already dropped an [EF1 tornado](https://twitter.com/NWSLittleRock/status/1244435167457886209) between the towns of Algoa and Amagon, Arkansas, about 45 minutes earlier.

Damage appears to be widespread, but the human toll from the Jonesboro tornado was remarkably low: only 22 people were injured, with just two of them hospitalized, as [reported](https://weather.com/news/news/2020-03-28-severe-weather-tornado-impacts-plains-south-midwest) by weather.com. The twister developed right over a dense commercial district on what would have normally been a weekend afternoon packed with shoppers and vehicles. Even though the state of Arkansas [has not yet implemented](https://www.kcur.org/post/resisting-calls-stay-home-order-governor-pushes-personal-responsibility#stream/0) a stay-at-home order in response to the coronavirus pandemic, many businesses in Jonesboro were already shuttered, including a mall that suffered major damage.

While the coronavirus shutdown may have saved lives in Jonesboro, it is complicating recovery efforts, as [reported](https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/29/us/tornado-coronavirus-arkansas.html) by the New York Times. With social distancing guidelines ruling the day, residents cannot gather as they normally would in churches and community centers for mutual support and information exchange. “You do what you have to do to meet the need at the moment, and right now, this is what we’re doing,” city councilman Bobby Long told the Times. “We’re doing our best to keep the virus under control. We will not abandon those people who need us the most at this time.”

The coronavirus-related shutdown has also thrown monkey wrenches into the clean-up effort after the deadly tornadoes that hit the Nashville area on March 3, [according to](https://www.csmonitor.com/USA/2020/0327/When-tornadoes-are-only-the-first-of-your-worries) the Christian Science Monitor.

**An outbreak that underperformed**
-----------------------------------

Saturday was [expected](https://www.wunderground.com/cat6/serious-tornado-threat-widespread-large-hail-on-tap-for-saturday) to be a busy tornado day—and it was—but, thankfully, it fell short of its potential. As of Monday, the NOAA/NWS Storm Prediction Center had [logged](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/climo/reports/200328_rpts.html) 24 tornado reports for Saturday. Most of these were in Iowa and Illinois, where a fast-moving spring storm and a strong warm front had been expected to serve as focal points for tornado development.

Late-morning thunderstorms left more cloudiness than predicted across northern and central Illinois, which cut down on instability and reduced the extent and strength of the resulting tornadic supercells near the surface low and warm front. The NWS/Quad Cities office was still carrying out storm surveys on Monday, with at least one EF1 [confirmed](https://twitter.com/NWSQuadCities/status/1244346932790726656) near Leon Corners, Illinois. Several short-lived tornadoes in central Iowa were [rated EF0 or EF1](https://twitter.com/NWSDesMoines) by the NWS/Des Moines office, and at least two tornadoes could not be rated because they did not strike any damage indicators (buildings, utility poles, or other objects).

Instability was greater and wind shear was plentiful toward the south, where the day’s strongest tornadoes ended up forming. Along with the EF3 in Jonesboro, a [pair](https://twitter.com/NWSPaducah/status/1244668906817675264) of EF2 tornadoes from a long-lived supercell struck near the Ohio River, one near Henderson, Kentucky, and the other in and near Newburgh, Indiana, just southeast of Evansville. Both tornadoes damaged dozens of homes, [according to](https://www.weather.gov/pah/mar28svere) the NWS/Paducah office.

**A somewhat active tornado season thus far**
---------------------------------------------

The “[inflation-adjusted](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/adj.html)” tornado count of 189 for the year through March 29 is a bit above average, close to the 75th percentile in a long-term database. (The inflation adjustment takes into account the increase in tornado reports in recent decades as more of the weakest tornadoes are caught on camera.)

Without an inflation adjustment, January and February ranked as the [sixth busiest start](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/sotc/tornadoes/202002) to the tornado year in records going back to 1950, with a preliminary total of 117 tornado reports.

![Image 1: Article image](https://s.w-x.co/inflation-adjusted-tornadoes-1.1-3.29.20-930px.jpg)Annual tornado count for 2019 through March 29, together with percentiles from a longer-term database (1954-2007). (NOAA/NWS/SPC)

The tornado death toll for 2020 so far—33—is unusually high for the first three months of the year. Of that total, 25 deaths occurred in the outbreak of March 2-3 that brought deadly tornadoes to Middle Tennessee.

Just as August is too soon to know whether a full hurricane season will be a busy one, we’re only now shifting into the most active three months of tornado season. On average, roughly half of U.S. tornadoes occur from April through June.

Slight-risk areas were in place by midday Monday for both Monday and Tuesday. Severe storms may track across northern and western Texas and western Oklahoma [on Monday afternoon and evening](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/outlook/archive/2020/day1otlk_20200330_1630.html). The setup suggests a low tornado threat but a chance of very large hail. A somewhat greater severe threat, including tornadoes, may evolve [on Tuesday](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/outlook/archive/2020/day2otlk_20200330_1730.html) as the severe weather shifts into southern Mississippi, Alabama, and Georgia and the Florida Panhandle. See weather.com for a [frequently updated outlook.](https://weather.com/storms/severe/news/2020-03-28-severe-thunderstorms-heavy-rain-flooding-south-early-week)

In the pictures: The forecast maps showed a cold front barreling toward Arkansas from the Plains on 03/19/2020. Showers and thunderstorms were expected ahead of the front. A secondary front followed from the north the next day, with Canadian high pressure ("H") and cooler air to follow.

									By mid-March, with severe weather season in full swing, there had yet to be any tornadoes during the month. Our string of good luck was about to change on the 19th as another cold front barreled into the area.

												At 930 pm CDT...Strong to severe thunderstorms were along a line from Mount Ida to Clinton and Melbourne. Some storms have exhibited rotation, with Tornado Warnings issued at times. While individual storms were tracking to the northeast, the line was moving slowly east.#arwx pic.twitter.com/4wNANsyZIZ
												— NWS Little Rock (@NWSLittleRock) March 20, 2020

												In the video: The WSR-88D (Doppler Weather Radar) showed strong to severe thunderstorms along a line north and west of Little Rock (Pulaski County) at 930 pm CDT on 03/19/2020. Some storms exhibited rotation, and Tornado Warnings were issued at times.

									A line of strong to severe storms developed ahead of the front, with the most robust storms closest to the Missouri border after 600 pm CDT. One storm in particular went from southeast Boone County into southern Marion County and northwest Baxter County.

												In the picture: Two tornadoes (rated EF1/EF2) were confirmed in Baxter, Boone, and Marion Counties on 03/19/2020.

									The storm had strong rotation at times and it headed quickly to the northeast at 40 to 50 mph. There was plenty of chaos in the path of the storm, and no doubt that one or more tornadoes were in play.

												Garage Wall Collapsed/Outbuildings Destroyed Southwest of Everton (Boone County)
												Haybarn Ripped Apart South of Pyatt (Marion County)
												Tree Damage Along a Creek South of Pyatt (Marion County)
												Top Floor of House Collapsed and Deposited Downstream South of Pyatt (Marion County)
												Tree Fell Through a House West of Mountain Home (Baxter County)
												Trees Snapped West of Mountain Home (Baxter County)

												In the pictures: A couple of tornadoes (rated EF1/EF2) were responsible for property and tree damage from two miles southwest of Everton (Boone County) to three miles west of Mountain Home (Baxter County) on 03/19/2020.

									A house was damaged east of Everton (Boone County), and power lines were downed. Between Pyatt and Bruno (both in Marion County), several homes were damaged or destroyed with an injury reported. A school was also affected. A tree fell through a house west of Mountain Home (Baxter County).

									In the end, two tornadoes (rated EF1/EF2) were spawned in a three county area. Three more weak tornadoes (all rated EF1) were confirmed with separate storms from five miles north of Hector (Pope County) to six miles west-southwest of Rupert (Van Buren County), and from four miles northeast of Evening Shade to four miles north of Poughkeepsie (both in Sharp County). These tornadoes toppled trees and hit a couple of barns and outbuildings.

									Link of Interest

									Damage Survey Information

												After Little Rock picked up a whopping 0.01" of rain yesterday, that makes 11 consecutive days in a row with measurable rainfall. If Little Rock can measure at least 0.01" of rain today, we would tie the record for most days in a row with measurable rainfall. #arwx pic.twitter.com/uSXqqHOeD4
												— NWS Little Rock (@NWSLittleRock) March 20, 2020

												In the table: Through 03/19/2020, there were eleven consecutive days with measurable rain at Little Rock (Pulaski County).

									This event did not feature a lot of rain, and there was only 0.01 inch measured at Little Rock (Pulaski County) on the 19th. But, this was enough to make it eleven consecutive days with measurable precipitation. It was one day away from tying the all-time record of twelve days in a row. A trace of rain on the 20th ended the streak.

												In the picture: Record high temperatures on 03/26/2020.

									Toward the end of March, it started feeling like summer on the 26th. A warm front exited to the north of the state, and ushered in well above average temperatures in the 80s to lower 90s.

									The high of 91 degrees at Harrison (Boone County) shattered the previous daily record of 81 degrees set in 2012. At Little Rock (Pulaski County), the mercury hit 88 degrees. It had not been this toasty since 1907 on this day when it was 85 degrees.

									It is days like this that pushed monthly temperatures well above normal. Average temperatures in March were four to eight degrees warmer than usual.

												In the picture: The WSR-88D (Doppler Weather Radar) showed a supercell (storm with rotating updrafts) and its classic kidney bean shape near Amagon (Jackson County) at 418 pm CDT on 03/28/2020. The radar detected inbound winds (green) adjacent to outbound (red) winds, indicating turning aloft. A Tornado Warning was in effect at the time. This storm tracked to the northeast and arrived in Jonesboro (Craighead County) shortly before 500 pm CDT.

                                                                        It was still very mild on the 28th, and there was at least some potential of tornadoes (although tornadoes were most likely from Iowa to Illinois and Indiana). Precipitation behaved for the bulk of the day (not much happening). A large area of showers crossed Arkansas during the afternoon, and there were rumbles of thunder at times. But as rain headed into eastern sections of the state, things got interesting.
									Rotation picked up in one storm near Tupelo (Jackson County), and a Tornado Warning was issued at 359 pm CDT. About twenty minutes later, there were reports of roofs off of homes between Algoa and Amagon (both in Jackson County). Farm equipment storage buildings were dismantled, and trees were uprooted.

									A tornado was to blame, and was given a rating of EF1 (110 mph winds) by the National Weather Service in Little Rock (Pulaski County). The tornado dissipated close to the Poinsett County line (a path length of just over five miles).

												5:20 PM-Here is a look at the tornado that intensified and moved through Jonesboro, AR this evening around 5 PM. @NWSMemphis continues to monitor this storm as it moves northeast, very dangerous! #arwx pic.twitter.com/3OXFEszbuq
												— NWS Little Rock (@NWSLittleRock) March 28, 2020

												In the video: A tornado was captured (forty seconds into the clip) along Interstate 555 at Red Wolf Boulevard in Jonesboro (Craighead County) shortly before 500 pm CDT on 03/28/2020. The tornado widened quickly before tearing through the south/east side of town. The video is courtesy of the Arkansas Department of Transportation.

									Rotation weakened temporarily, but cranked up again (30 miles to the northeast) as the storm arrived on the south/east side of Jonesboro (Craighead County) shortly before 500 pm CDT. Numerous homes and businesses (including a mall) were heavily damaged or destroyed, and cars were tossed like toys. Hangers and planes were ripped up at the airport, and a 74 mph gust was measured by observing equipment. Just north of the airport, a train was derailed. At least twenty people were injured, but there were no casualties.
                                                                        Due to the coronavirus pandemic, there was not much going on around town. Stores were either closed or experiencing much lighter than normal traffic. According to officials, areas that were affected by the tornado would have been crowded, and this situation (from a fatality/injury standpoint) could have been much worse.

												Detailed survey information for tornado damage tracks in Craighead and Greene Counties: https://t.co/1RvjJIN9uy pic.twitter.com/93rQDzV8k1 #arwx
												— NWS Memphis (@NWSMemphis) March 30, 2020

												In the picture: A damage survey team from the National Weather Service in Memphis, TN confirmed two tornadoes in northeast Arkansas on 03/28/2020. The Jonesboro (Craighead County) tornado was given a preliminary rating of EF3 (maximum winds around 140 mph).

									The nightmare did not end at Jonesboro (Craighead County). The storm traveled through Brookland (Craighead County) and just east of Paragould (Greene County), and caused more mayhem.
									A damage survey by the National Weather Service in Memphis, TN confirmed an EF3 tornado (140 mph winds) at Jonesboro (Craighead County). This was the strongest tornado in the state since the EF4 monster twister that pummeled Mayflower and Vilonia (both in Faulkner County) on April 27, 2014. A separate tornado (rated EF1) was identified in southeast Greene County (a total of three tornadoes during the event).

JONESBORO ARKANSAS TORNADO 2020: A WARNING SUCCESS STORY

![Image 3: tornado in sky](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0531/2856/0817/articles/1daf482d2ba735a10d06889e2cde584c_aabd7eb2-ab14-4c8f-9c36-7585ed539fc2.jpg?v=1746477120&width=1800)

Table of Contents
-----------------

*   [No Fatalities Reported](https://midlandusa.com/blogs/blog/jonesboro-arkansas-tornado-a-warning-success-story?srsltid=AfmBOor49BflJ75c1q4HJ2opnJMU3rfV2UzfUq171x1zRYBSUT6Qh0G9#no-fatalities-reported)
*   [Tracking the Tornado](https://midlandusa.com/blogs/blog/jonesboro-arkansas-tornado-a-warning-success-story?srsltid=AfmBOor49BflJ75c1q4HJ2opnJMU3rfV2UzfUq171x1zRYBSUT6Qh0G9#tracking-the-tornado)

A Tornado Warning Success Story
===============================

On Saturday, March 28, 2020, ten minutes after the National Weather Service issued its warning, a strong tornado with top winds estimated at 140mph, plowed a twelve mile long path through portions of Jonesboro, AR. The Jonesboro Arkansas Tornado in 2020 damaged or destroyed more than 200 homes and businesses, including Turtle Creek Mall and the city airport.

No Fatalities Reported
----------------------

Eighteen people were injured, but amazingly, no one was killed. Isolation due to the COVID-19 coronavirus meant the mall and other businesses were much less crowded than they would have been on a typical Saturday afternoon. Most importantly, the tornado warning was issued at 4:47 pm and the twister touched down at 4:57pm, meaning those ten minutes allowed everyone plenty of time to seek shelter and survive.

Tracking the Tornado
--------------------

The National Weather Service damage survey found that the twister touched down just north of Interstate highway 555, produced EF-2 damage at the Mall, then strengthened to EF-3 force as it destroyed buildings and airplanes at the Jonesboro Airport and beyond. At its widest, the funnel left a swath of damage one-third of a mile across, along a path of more than twelve miles.

Early Warning Was Key
---------------------

Occurring on a March day (the middle of Arkansas’ tornado season), just before 5pm (the most common time of day for Arkansas tornadoes), and two hours after Tornado Watch #68 had been issued for the area, the tornado was not unexpected, meaning the people of Jonesboro were well aware of the day’s severe weather risk. Warnings from the National Weather Service via weather radio and cell phone, combined with outstanding on-air coverage by local television and radio stations undoubtedly saved lives. As the 2020 tornado season kicks in, everyone can learn a good lesson from the Jonesboro tornado: know your risk for severe weather, have multiple redundant methods of receiving warnings, watch your local TV station’s storm coverage, and have a practiced, well-understood plan of action to get to your safe place.  
  
Every home, school, and business should have a [Midland NOAA Weather Alert Radio](https://midlandusa.com/collections/weather).  As the official “Voice of the National Weather Service”, it keeps you informed and alerted no matter what you’re doing. Buy it, plug it in, and be prepared.

Abstract
--------

On March 28, 2020, a tornado developed in southeast Jonesboro and traveled northeast through the city damaging about 300 buildings. There were 22 injuries but fortunately, no fatalities, which is remarkable given that the tornado traveled through a densely populated area on Saturday afternoon. The next day, the authors surveyed the damage assigning degrees of damage (DoD) to multiple damage indicators (DIs) in accordance with the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale (WSEC, 2006). The EF-Scale was written in 2006 and adopted by the National Weather Service (NWS) in 2007. In this event, NWS personnel plotted the damage locations on the damage assessment toolkit (DAT) and assigned a maximum damage rating of EF 3 to this tornado.

Key takeaways

![Image 7: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)AI




-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  The tornado on March 28, 2020, resulted in damage to approximately 300 buildings in Jonesboro, AR.
2.  The tornado reached a maximum damage rating of EF 3, with an estimated wind speed of 61 m/s (136 mph).
3.  Damage surveys revealed the tornado path extended 20 km (12.6 mi) and had a maximum width of 550 m (1800 ft).
4.  Documentation of large shopping malls is lacking; this survey aims to address that for the EF-scale update.
5.  The survey involved more than 80 scientists to standardize the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale for future tornado assessments.

A tornado outbreak occurred during the evening of 26 December 2015 across portions of North Texas. In all, there were 12 confirmed tornadoes in 8 counties. Unfortunately, 13 people lost their lives and there were numerous injuries as two of the strongest tornadoes struck Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW) suburbs. Most fatalities occurred in vehicles near the Interstate 30/George Bush Turnpike interchange in Garland, Texas (Fig. 1). Damage survey teams were dispatched the next day by the Fort Worth National Weather Service (FWD) to determine characteristics of the tornado paths. The survey team utilized the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale to rate damage severity developed by the Wind Science and Engineering Research Center (WSERC, 2006). This scale lists increasing degrees of damage (DoDs) to 28 damage indicators (DIs). DIs involved various building types as well as other items. The EF scale was adopted by the National Weather Service (NWS) in 2007. Not surprisingly, we found that tornadoes exploited construction deficiencies in building connections, sometimes causing more severe building damage. Therefore, we adjusted EF ratings downward where there was poor construction. The damage survey team found two major tornado tracks near Dallas, Texas. One tornado traveled from Midlothian to Ovilla to Glenn Heights and will be referred to herein as the MOG tornado. This tornado traveled 14 km, was up to 110 m wide, with maximum damage intensity of EF3. The other major tornado, produced by a second supercell, traveled from Sunnyvale to Garland to Rowlett and will be referred to herein as the SGR tornado. This tornado traveled about 21 km, was up to 500 m wide, with maximum damage intensity of EF4.

JONESBORO, Ark. — A tornado ripped through northeast Arkansas on Saturday, leaving six people hurt after hitting commercial and residential areas in the college town of Jonesboro.

The six people reported injured were taken to a local hospital with minor juries, Jonesboro E-911 Director Jeff Presley said. The tornado did major damage at the Mall at Turtle Creek and Jonesboro Municipal Airport.

Like much of the rest of the world, Jonesboro is working to fight the spread of COVID-19. Because of that, most stores in the Mall at Turtle Creek were closed Saturday to fight the coronavirus pandemic.

Severe weather could have been much worse if not for that, Presley said.

“At 5 o’clock on a Saturday afternoon that place would’ve been packed, and at this point there was hardly anyone in there,” Presley said. “It’s a blessing in disguise.”

Power was out in sections of the city, which affects the city’s traffic lights. Wreckage tossed about by the twister also blocked roads. They mayor issued a 7 p.m. curfew, and authorities asked people not to drive around.

The storm also derailed a train, Presley said. Crews were examining damage and trying to determine whether there it had been hauling anything hazardous.

The National Weather Service tweeted a video from the Arkansas Department of Transportation that showed a large tornado dropping from storm clouds in Jonesboro.

U.S. Rep. Rick Crawford, who represents much of eastern Arkansas, said on Twitter that a tornado tore through “the heart of town” and asked for prayers for first responders. Crawford said his staff and family were safe.

Jonesboro is home to Arkansas State University. The university tweeted that campus was not damaged.

Forecasters with the Storm Prediction Center in Norman, Oklahoma, warned that a severe weather outbreak was possible later Saturday for much of the central U.S.

The National Weather Service reported other possible tornadoes Saturday in Illinois and Iowa.

LITTLE ROCK (KATV) — Governor Asa Hutchinson declares a state disaster in the Jonesboro area after an EF3 tornado Saturday night and called for federal assistance to rebuild the area.

“I want to assure all of Jonesboro and Northeast Arkansas that the entire state has been in prayer. I have not seen this kind of devastation from a tornado since I have been governor," said Hutchinson.

All of the businesses destroyed by the Jonesboro tornado qualify for COVID-19 disaster loans, according to the governor.

Major damage to homes- in the Wildwood-after a tornado touched down in Jonesboro. (Video credit: Live Streams Media/ Adair-Clement)

Officials said The Red Cross is about 35 percent complete with assessing tornado damage in Jonesboro. 55 homes were completely destroyed and will need to be rebuilt.

Gov. Hutchinson said the state is waiting to find out if the damage reached the threshold to declare the tornado a federal disaster, to get assistance from FEMA. He believes it does meet the federal requirement for aid

Officials reportedly said the two people were required to be hospitalized with non-life threatening injuries, and no casualties have been reported.

Crews on Airport Road reported no injuries and only minor gas leaks from a few cars that were thrown upsidedown. Jonesboro Airport has also been searched and cleared.

Two airplanes there will require heavy machinery in order to move. Camfil, located at 3505 Airport Rd., has also been searched and cleared with the factory taking a direct hit, according to Region 8.

The family behind [a viral Northeast Arkansas mom's photo](https://katv.com/news/local/the-story-behind-a-viral-photo-of-an-arkansas-doctor-and-his-son) shows that shows her son and husband separated by a glass door, have lost their home in the tornado.

Dr. Jared Burks has been living apart from his wife Alyssa and their son Zeke while he treats patients during the coronavirus pandemic.

Jared, Alyssa and their son Zeke are okay and have set up a go fund me page, to donate, click [here](https://www.gofundme.com/f/1yo5w210mo).

Aerial tornado damage video in Jonesboro. Video: Live Storms Media/Brent Adair)

The Arkansas Army National Guard delivered 200 cots to assist the city of Jonesboro to facilitate shelter operations after a Saturday's tornado, said the agency in a press release.

The 875th Engineer Battalion delivered the cots just after midnight. The Guard said it stands ready to assist further if officials need help.

The city has set up four shelters for people to use. They include University Heights, Fox Meadow and Nettleton STEAM Schools as well as Journey Church on Disciple Drive in Jonesboro.

Aerial damage of airport, Turtle Creek Mall, and train deraining in Jonesboro. (Video: KAIT8)

The City of Jonesboro is reportedly under a new curfew,9 p.m. -6 a.m., from Sunday night into Monday morning.

Officials say their best estimate for damage costs: “several hundred million dollars."

For those seeking aid for damage from the Jonesboro tornado, call (501) 935-5561.

Jonesboro Tornado Five Year Anniversary: Journey’s
==================================================

When the tornado tore through Jonesboro, it took out one of the staples of the city, the Mall at Turtle Creek.

By [Alejandra Hernández](https://www.kait8.com/authors/alejandra-hernandez/)

Published: Mar. 28, 2025 at 5:30 PM CDT

JONESBORO, Ark. (KAIT) - When the tornado tore through Jonesboro, it took out one of the staples of the city: The Mall at Turtle Creek.

Five years later, some of those stores are still gone, but some have taken a long journey to come back.

Anna Treece manages Journeys at Caraway Plaza. She was also the store’s manager in 2020 when it was at the mall.

“It’s so crazy. COVID. Everyone talks about that period. COVID was secondary for me at that time. The tornado was what changed my life, turned it upside down,” she said. “Five o’clock on a Saturday is always a busy time for malls.”

However, the mall was closed due to COVID-19.

On a regular Saturday, she would have been at the store. Instead, Treece was at home watching K8’s storm coverage on TV.

“We knew there was bad weather in the area, but thankfully most of the employees and customers were not inside the mall that day,” she said.

She remembered the moment she saw the tornado hit the mall.

“The moment that I saw the tornado hit the mall, it was pretty devastating, not gonna lie,” she said.

The mall suffered significant damage. Many stores were nearly leveled, including Journeys.

Treece and her employees were never allowed to go back and see the damage with their own eyes.

“I’ve seen pictures. It definitely was a blessing we weren’t there,” she said. “Some things were left in place, and then other things were just completely in disarray or missing. The wires were hanging out. It was flooded.”

Treece called her company, trying to find a way to get the store back. But the company wasn’t operating outside of malls at the time. As time would tell, the mall would not come back.

“You hear a lot of people say malls are a dying thing, but we actually had a lot of stores in our mall that were tops in their company, ours being one,” she said. “We had come off of having the best year ever, into not having a store at all. And so, it was hard. It was hard trying to figure out what to do next.”

What comes next?

For Treece, it wasn’t an easy answer. She was on furlough for months, then on unemployment.

Almost a year later, the store still wasn’t back in Jonesboro.

Treece made a difficult choice to travel to Memphis and work at a Journeys there.

“I missed my Journeys family. I wanted to be back with my customers. I wanted to be back with my colleagues. There was no light at the end of the tunnel,” she said. “I decided to make a change, start the drive. Then the bridge was out during that time. So, \[the commute\] would take two to three hours. One day it took me six hours to get to work.”

About a year later, and growing more homesick, Treece left Journeys.

“It was a good experience, but it was a hard experience. It was very rewarding, but it got to even though I was driving home at night, I was leaving early in the morning. I got really homesick for Northeast Arkansas,” she said.

Treece left Journeys, but Journeys never left her.

Journeys was testing stores outside of malls. A month after she left, she got the call she’d been waiting three years for.

“I fought really hard to get this store back. I would find locations. I would send pictures in. It was kind of back and forth and in the end, when I got the call, it just felt like a victory. It felt like, ‘Okay, I’m going to be home again.’ This is home for me.”

Treece said many of her employees at the mall also came back with her.

“It was nice because we got to open it together,” she said. “Not very many of us came back after the mall was destroyed. So, it’s a blessing to be able to see customers walk through the door and say, ‘Oh my goodness, I remember you from the mall.‘”

Journeys relocated to Caraway Plaza in 2023, Treece said she’s built a new team that she’s happy to call her family.

The week before this interview, Treece said her store won district store of the year.

“I knew there was going to be a way somehow, someday, and we made it happen,” she said.
